lines.text: Car insurance prices jumped about 64% in five years.
lines.say: Car insurance prices jumped about sixty-four percent in five years.

lines.text: And then, in 2026, they started falling. Home insurance didn't.
lines.say: And then, in twenty twenty-six, they started falling. Home insurance didn't.

lines.text: Over those same five years, overall prices rose about 24%. Insurance ran way ahead.
lines.say: Over those same five years, overall prices rose about twenty-four percent. Insurance ran way ahead.

lines.text: So what happened? Was it greed, disasters, fancy cars, or lawyers?
lines.say: So what happened? Was it greed? Disasters? Fancy cars? Lawyers?

lines.text: The answer is a little bit of each, and it shows up in the math insurers use.
lines.say: The answer is a little bit of each, and it all shows up in the math insurers use.

lines.text: Let's open the black box, one bill at a time: car, home, health, and what you can actually control.
lines.say: Let's open the black box, one bill at a time. Car, home, health, and what you can actually control.

lines.text: Chapter one: how insurance pricing works.
lines.say: Chapter one. How insurance pricing works.

lines.text: Insurance is a pool. Lots of people pay in a little, so the few who crash or burn out get a lot.
lines.say: Insurance is a pool. Lots of people pay in a little, so the few who crash, or have a fire, get a lot.

lines.text: Your premium is your share of the pool's expected bill, plus the cost of running the company.
lines.say: Your premium is your share of the pool's expected bill, plus the cost of running the company.

lines.text: Here's a simple example. Picture 1,000 drivers in one pool.
lines.say: Here's a simple example. Picture a thousand drivers in one pool.

lines.text: Each year, about 50 of them file a claim, and the average claim costs $10,000.
lines.say: Each year, about fifty of them file a claim, and the average claim costs ten thousand dollars.

lines.text: That's $500,000 in claims, or $500 per driver, before the insurer pays a single salary.
lines.say: That's five hundred thousand dollars in claims. Or five hundred dollars per driver, before the insurer pays a single salary.

lines.text: If costs and profit take 25% of the premium, the price has to be about $667.
lines.say: If costs and profit take twenty-five percent of the premium, the price has to be about six sixty-seven.

lines.text: Now make the average claim 30% pricier: $13,000 instead of $10,000.
lines.say: Now make the average claim thirty percent pricier. Thirteen thousand dollars, instead of ten.

lines.text: Same drivers, same crashes, and the premium jumps from $667 to about $867.
lines.say: Same drivers, same number of crashes, and the premium jumps from six sixty-seven to about eight sixty-seven.

lines.text: That's the key: you can drive perfectly and still pay more, because the pool costs more.
lines.say: That's the key. You can drive perfectly and still pay more, because the whole pool costs more.

lines.text: The same logic runs home and health insurance. When the average claim rises, everyone's share rises.
lines.say: The same logic runs home and health insurance. When the average claim rises, everyone's share rises with it.

lines.text: Insurers track all this with one number, the combined ratio: claims plus expenses, divided by premiums.
lines.say: Insurers track all this with one number, called the combined ratio. It's claims plus expenses, divided by premiums.

lines.text: Under 100 means they made money on policies. Over 100 means they paid out more than they took in.
lines.say: Under a hundred means they made money on the policies. Over a hundred means they paid out more than they took in.

lines.text: Insurers also invest premiums until claims are paid, but the core test is still that ratio.
lines.say: Insurers also invest the premiums until claims are paid. But the core scorecard is still that ratio.

lines.text: Keep that number in mind. It explains almost everything that happened next.
lines.say: Keep that number in mind. It explains almost everything that happened next.

lines.text: Chapter two: the car insurance spike.
lines.say: Chapter two. The car insurance spike.

lines.text: Here's how car insurance prices changed each year, from the Consumer Price Index.
lines.say: Here's how car insurance prices changed each year, according to the Consumer Price Index.

lines.text: In 2020, people stayed home, crashes dropped, and prices fell 4.8%.
lines.say: In twenty twenty, people stayed home, crashes dropped, and prices fell four point eight percent.

lines.text: Then 2023 hit: up 20.3% in a year, the biggest jump since 1976.
lines.say: Then came twenty twenty-three. Up twenty point three percent in a year, the biggest jump since nineteen seventy-six.

lines.text: From December 2020 to December 2025, that stacks up to about 64%.
lines.say: From December twenty twenty to December twenty twenty-five, those years stack up to about sixty-four percent.

lines.text: Why so fast? First, cars got expensive to fix.
lines.say: Why so fast? First, cars got expensive to fix.

lines.text: A bumper isn't just plastic anymore. It hides cameras and sensors that need parts and calibration.
lines.say: A bumper isn't just plastic anymore. It hides cameras and sensors that need new parts and careful calibration.

lines.text: The average repair estimate went from about 11 replacement parts in 2020 to about 13.5 in 2024.
lines.say: The average repair estimate went from about eleven replacement parts in twenty twenty, to about thirteen and a half in twenty twenty-four.

lines.text: CCC found parts drove more than half of the rise in repair costs.
lines.say: And C C C found that parts drove more than half of the rise in repair costs.

lines.text: The price index for car repair and maintenance climbed 43.6% from January 2019 to January 2025.
lines.say: The price index for car repair and maintenance climbed about forty-four percent from January twenty nineteen to January twenty twenty-five.

lines.text: Used car prices also soared in 2021 and 2022, so totaled cars cost more to replace.
lines.say: Used car prices also soared in twenty twenty-one and twenty twenty-two, so totaled cars cost more to replace.

lines.text: And more crashes end with the car written off. Total losses hit a record 23% of claims, says CCC.
lines.say: And more crashes now end with the car written off. Total losses hit a record twenty-three percent of claims, according to C C C.

scene.label: Claims ending in a total loss

lines.text: Second, injuries got pricier. The average bodily injury payout hit $27,373 in 2024.
lines.say: Second, injuries got pricier. The average bodily injury payout hit about twenty-seven thousand four hundred dollars in twenty twenty-four.

lines.text: And repairs take longer when parts are scarce, so rental-car bills on claims run longer too.
lines.say: And repairs take longer when parts are scarce, so the rental-car part of a claim runs longer too.

lines.text: Insurers also point to bigger lawsuits and settlements, which they call legal system abuse.
lines.say: Insurers also point to bigger lawsuits and settlements, which the industry calls legal system abuse.

scene.source: Insurance Information Institute term for rising litigation costs

lines.text: Third, insurers were losing money. Personal auto's combined ratio was 112.2 in 2022.
lines.say: Third, insurers were losing money. Personal auto's combined ratio was a hundred twelve point two in twenty twenty-two.

lines.text: That's $112.20 out the door for every $100 of premium. The industry lost $33.1 billion on car policies that year.
lines.say: That's a hundred twelve dollars and twenty cents out the door for every hundred dollars of premium. The industry lost thirty-three billion dollars on car policies that year.

lines.text: And price hikes need state approval, so increases arrived late and piled up.
lines.say: And in most states, price hikes need regulator approval, so the increases arrived late and piled up.

lines.text: To catch up, the industry's written premiums grew 14.4% in 2023 and 12.8% in 2024.
lines.say: To catch up, the industry's written premiums grew fourteen point four percent in twenty twenty-three, and twelve point eight percent in twenty twenty-four.

lines.text: By 2024, the combined ratio fell to 95.3. In 2025, 91.8, the best since the pandemic.
lines.say: By twenty twenty-four, the combined ratio fell to ninety-five point three. In twenty twenty-five, ninety-one point eight, the best since the pandemic.

lines.text: Profitable again, insurers started competing for drivers. Price growth slowed to 2.8% in 2025.
lines.say: Profitable again, insurers started competing for drivers. Price growth slowed to two point eight percent in twenty twenty-five.

lines.text: And by August 2026, car insurance prices were down 5.1% from a year earlier.
lines.say: And by August twenty twenty-six, car insurance prices were down five point one percent from a year earlier.

scene.label: Car insurance prices, Aug 2026 vs a year earlier

lines.text: That's the car story: costs jumped, insurers lost money, prices caught up, and now they're easing.
lines.say: That's the car story. Costs jumped, insurers lost money, prices caught up, and now they're easing.

lines.text: Chapter three: why home insurance keeps climbing.
lines.say: Chapter three. Why home insurance keeps climbing.

lines.text: Your home policy pays mostly for fire, wind, hail and storms. And those got expensive.
lines.say: Your home policy pays mostly for fire, wind, hail and storms. And those got expensive.

lines.text: In 2024, the US had 27 weather disasters that each cost at least a billion dollars.
lines.say: In twenty twenty-four, the US had twenty-seven weather disasters that each cost at least a billion dollars.

lines.text: Together they cost $182.7 billion. Only 2023, with 28, had more events.
lines.say: Together they cost a hundred eighty-two point seven billion dollars. Only twenty twenty-three, with twenty-eight, had more events.

lines.text: Globally, insured disaster losses topped $100 billion for the sixth straight year in 2025: $107 billion.
lines.say: Globally, insured disaster losses topped a hundred billion dollars for the sixth straight year in twenty twenty-five. A hundred seven billion.

scene.label: Insured natural catastrophe losses, 2025
scene.sub: sixth year over $100B; 83% in the US (Swiss Re)

lines.text: That was actually down 24% from 2024's $141 billion, and still one of the costliest years on record.
lines.say: That was actually down twenty-four percent from twenty twenty-four's hundred forty-one billion. And still one of the costliest years on record.

lines.text: And 83% of those losses were in the United States.
lines.say: And eighty-three percent of those losses were in the United States.

lines.text: A record 92% of 2025's insured losses came from so-called secondary perils: wildfires, hail, floods and severe storms.
lines.say: A record ninety-two percent of twenty twenty-five's insured losses came from so-called secondary perils: wildfires, hail, floods and severe storms.

scene.label: Share of 2025 insured losses from secondary perils

lines.text: Those aren't once-a-century hurricanes. They're frequent, smaller disasters that add up every year.
lines.say: Those aren't once-a-century hurricanes. They're frequent, smaller disasters that add up every single year.

lines.text: The Los Angeles wildfires in January 2025 alone caused about $40 billion of insured losses.
lines.say: The Los Angeles wildfires in January twenty twenty-five alone caused about forty billion dollars of insured losses.

scene.headline: LA wildfires: largest insured wildfire loss on record

lines.text: Now meet the insurer's insurer: reinsurance. You pay your insurer, and your insurer pays a reinsurer to cover its biggest risks.
lines.say: Now meet the insurer's insurer. Reinsurance. You pay your insurer, and your insurer pays a reinsurer to cover its own biggest risks.

lines.text: Insurers buy it so one huge storm doesn't wipe them out. And its price exploded.
lines.say: Insurers buy it so one huge storm doesn't wipe them out. And its price exploded.

lines.text: At the January 2023 renewals, US property catastrophe reinsurance rates jumped 31.3%, the biggest one-year rise since 2006.
lines.say: At the January twenty twenty-three renewals, US property catastrophe reinsurance rates jumped thirty-one point three percent. The biggest one-year rise since two thousand six.

scene.label: US property cat reinsurance rates, Jan 2023

lines.text: Over six straight years of increases, that index nearly doubled.
lines.say: Over six straight years of increases, that index nearly doubled.

scene.label: US property cat reinsurance rates, 2017 to 2023

lines.text: Add pricier lumber and labor to rebuild, and your premium has three new costs baked in.
lines.say: Add pricier lumber and labor to rebuild, and your premium has three new costs baked in.

lines.text: Some insurers simply stopped selling. In May 2023, State Farm stopped taking new home applications in California.
lines.say: Some insurers simply stopped selling. In May twenty twenty-three, State Farm stopped taking new home applications in California.

scene.headline: State Farm stops new homeowners applications in California

lines.text: It cited wildfire risk, construction costs and the reinsurance market.
lines.say: It cited wildfire risk, construction costs, and a challenging reinsurance market.

lines.text: In September 2026, State Farm filed rules that could let it consider new California applications from fire-hardened homes.
lines.say: In September twenty twenty-six, State Farm filed rules that could let it consider new California applications again, from homes that meet wildfire-resilience standards.

scene.headline: State Farm files to reopen some California home policies

lines.text: Fewer sellers means less competition, and fewer cheap options for homeowners.
lines.say: Fewer sellers means less competition, and fewer cheap options for homeowners.

lines.text: One industry estimate puts the average home premium at $2,948 in 2025, up 12% in a year.
lines.say: One industry estimate puts the average home premium at about two thousand nine hundred fifty dollars in twenty twenty-five, up twelve percent in a year.

lines.text: The same estimate says home insurance costs rose about 46% since 2021, roughly three times overall inflation.
lines.say: The same estimate says home insurance costs rose about forty-six percent since twenty twenty-one. Roughly three times overall inflation.

lines.text: And it hits renters and buyers too, because landlords and mortgage lenders pass it along.
lines.say: And it hits renters and buyers too, because landlords and lenders build insurance into the monthly cost.

lines.text: Chapter four: the bill you might not see.
lines.say: Chapter four. The bill you might not see.

scene.title: The bill you might not see

lines.text: If you get health insurance through work, the full price is mostly hidden from you.
lines.say: If you get health insurance through work, the full price is mostly hidden from you.

lines.text: In 2025, the average family plan cost $26,993, up 6% in a year.
lines.say: In twenty twenty-five, the average family plan cost twenty-six thousand nine hundred ninety-three dollars, up six percent in a year.

lines.text: Workers paid $6,850 of that directly. Employers paid the rest.
lines.say: Workers paid six thousand eight hundred fifty of that directly. Employers paid the rest.

lines.text: That 6% jump outpaced both wage growth, at 4%, and inflation, at 2.7%, according to KFF.
lines.say: That six percent jump outpaced both wage growth, at four percent, and inflation, at two point seven, according to K F F.

lines.text: But economists generally find that employer-paid premiums come partly out of what would have been wages.
lines.say: But economists generally find that employer-paid premiums come partly out of what could have been your raise.

lines.text: So even the part you don't see can shape your paycheck.
lines.say: So even the part you don't see can shape your paycheck.

lines.text: Wait, so is it just greed? The numbers are messier than that.
lines.say: Wait, so is it just greed? The numbers are messier than that.

lines.text: Car insurers lost $33.1 billion on policies in 2022. In 2025, a 91.8 ratio meant about 8 cents of underwriting profit per premium dollar.
lines.say: Car insurers lost thirty-three billion dollars on policies in twenty twenty-two. In twenty twenty-five, a ninety-one point eight ratio meant about eight cents of underwriting profit per premium dollar.

lines.text: And in most states, regulators review rate increases before they take effect. Prices chase costs, with a lag.
lines.say: And in most states, regulators review rate increases before they take effect. Prices chase costs, with a lag.

lines.text: Chapter five: what you can actually control.
lines.say: Chapter five. What you can actually control.

lines.text: You can't stop hailstorms. But a few levers do move your price.
lines.say: You can't stop hailstorms. But a few levers do move your price.

lines.text: Lever one: prices for the same driver can differ a lot from one insurer to the next.
lines.say: Lever one. Prices for the same driver can differ a lot from one insurer to the next.

lines.text: Each company weighs your car, ZIP code and driving record differently, so comparing quotes is the classic first move.
lines.say: Each company weighs your car, ZIP code and driving record differently. So comparing quotes is the classic first move.

lines.text: Just compare the same coverage. A cheaper quote can mean lower limits or a bigger deductible.
lines.say: Just compare the same coverage. A cheaper quote can hide lower limits, or a bigger deductible.

lines.text: Lever two: the deductible, the part you pay before insurance kicks in.
lines.say: Lever two. The deductible, the part you pay before insurance kicks in.

lines.text: A higher deductible usually means a lower premium, because you're taking on more of the small claims.
lines.say: A higher deductible usually means a lower premium, because you're taking on more of the small claims yourself.

lines.text: The catch: you need that deductible in cash if something happens. It's a trade-off, not free money.
lines.say: The catch: you need that deductible in cash if something happens. It's a trade-off, not free money.

scene.label: Cash you'd need after a claim

lines.text: Example: say a higher deductible saves $200 a year. Three claim-free years saves $600, but one claim costs $500 more out of pocket.
lines.say: Here's an example. Say a higher deductible saves you two hundred dollars a year. Three claim-free years saves six hundred, but one claim costs you five hundred more out of pocket.

lines.text: Lever three: bundling home and car with one company often earns a discount.
lines.say: Lever three. Bundling home and car with one company often earns a discount.

lines.text: Lever four: discounts for things like safe-driving apps, home security, or a new roof.
lines.say: Lever four. Discounts for things like safe-driving apps, home security, or a new roof.

lines.text: And in most states, your credit-based insurance score affects car rates. A few states, like California, Hawaii and Massachusetts, don't allow it.
lines.say: And in most states, your credit-based insurance score affects car rates. A few states, like California, Hawaii and Massachusetts, don't allow that.

lines.text: None of these change the disasters. But they change how much of the pool's bill lands on you.
lines.say: None of these change the disasters. But they change how much of the pool's bill lands on you.

lines.text: Chapter six: the recap.
lines.say: Chapter six. The recap.

lines.text: One: insurance prices follow the cost of claims. When claims get pricier, everyone in the pool pays.
lines.say: One. Insurance prices follow the cost of claims. When claims get pricier, everyone in the pool pays.

lines.text: Two: car insurance rose about 64% from 2020 to 2025, as repairs, injuries and losses piled up, and it's now easing.
lines.say: Two. Car insurance rose about sixty-four percent from twenty twenty to twenty twenty-five, as repairs, injuries and losses piled up. Now it's easing.

lines.text: Three: home insurance keeps rising with disasters, reinsurance and rebuilding costs.
lines.say: Three. Home insurance keeps rising with disasters, reinsurance and rebuilding costs.

lines.text: Four: you can't control the weather, but quotes, deductibles, bundles and discounts change your share.
lines.say: And four. You can't control the weather, but quotes, deductibles, bundles and discounts change your share.

lines.text: Insurance isn't magic. It's a giant shared bill, and now you know how it's split.
lines.say: Insurance isn't magic. It's a giant shared bill, and now you know how it gets split.

post.title: Car insurance jumped 64% in 5 years. Here's why insurance got so expensive
post.ig: Car insurance prices rose about 64% from 2020 to 2025. Here's why, and why home insurance keeps climbing.
post.tiktok: Car insurance +64% in five years, now easing. Home insurance still climbing. Here's the math.
post.yt_desc:
Car insurance prices rose about 64% from December 2020 to December 2025, including a 20.3% jump in 2023, the biggest since 1976, before falling 5.1% in the year to August 2026. We explain how insurance pricing works with simple pool math, why car repairs and injury claims got pricier, why disasters and reinsurance keep pushing home insurance up, what job-based health premiums really cost, and the levers people use to change their share.
